kf: **Actinic (solar) keratoses** are UV-induced patches of dysplastic keratinocytes on chronically sun-exposed skin.
Very common: up to **25% of people over 60** in northern England and Ireland; more in fair skin, outdoor workers and the immunosuppressed.
Rough, **gritty** scale on a pink base, often easier to feel than see; face, bald scalp, ears, forearms and backs of hands.
A single AK rarely becomes SCC, but people with **many AKs** have a 10–15% lifetime SCC risk (field cancerisation).
Sun protection for all; cryotherapy for few lesions; **field treatment** (5-FU, imiquimod, diclofenac 3%, PDT). Tender, thick or growing → exclude SCC.

sub: Older adults with fair skin (Fitzpatrick I–II), chronic sun exposure and photoageing.
Organ transplant recipients and other immunosuppressed people have many more, and more aggressive, lesions.
Individual AKs can regress (up to a quarter a year), persist or, rarely, progress to SCC.

aet: Cumulative **UVB** (and UVA) exposure: outdoor work, sunbeds, living in sunny climates.
Immunosuppression (transplant drugs), older age, previous skin cancer; HPV types may contribute.
myths: **"It's just dry skin"**: a persistent gritty patch on sun-damaged skin is an AK until shown otherwise.
**"Treat each spot"**: once cancer is excluded, treating the whole field matters more.
patho_lead: UV damage to keratinocyte DNA creates a **field** of genetically abnormal cells; the AK is the visible tip.

mech.t: UVB forms pyrimidine dimers; mutations in **TP53** let damaged keratinocytes survive and divide.
Mutated clones spread along the basal layer, producing **dysplasia** of the lower epidermis.
mech.cap: Actinic keratosis (left: rough scale over dysplastic epidermis) compared with a benign seborrhoeic keratosis (right).

mech.t: Dysplastic cells make abnormal keratin, giving adherent, rough **parakeratotic** scale.
Surrounding sun-damaged skin carries similar mutations, so new AKs and SCCs arise across the field.
mech.cap: Multiple AKs across a sun-damaged bald scalp.

mech.t: If dysplasia becomes full-thickness (Bowen's disease) or invades the dermis, it has become SCC.

histo: Atypical keratinocytes in the **basal layer** (partial-thickness dysplasia), with parakeratosis that spares the follicular openings (alternating pink and blue).
Biopsy if thick, tender, ulcerated or not responding (to exclude SCC).

sub: Many AKs and high SCC risk: lower threshold for specialist referral and regular skin checks.
Blurred, scaly vermilion border of the lower lip; higher risk of SCC: lower threshold for specialist review.

comp: Inflammatory reactions to field treatments; cosmetic concern.
prog: Chronic: new lesions keep appearing in sun-damaged skin.
Treatment clears most lesions; ongoing sun protection and surveillance are needed.

quiz.q: Why treat a field of AKs rather than single spots?
quiz.a: The whole sun-damaged area carries mutated cells (field cancerisation); treating it reduces new AKs and SCCs.
Tenderness, thickening, induration, rapid growth, ulceration or bleeding.
Topical 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod and diclofenac 3% gel; photodynamic therapy via dermatology.

quiz.q: What should patients expect from 5-FU or imiquimod?
quiz.a: An inflammatory phase: redness, crusting and soreness before healing.
Actinic keratosis of the lip vermilion; higher risk of SCC.
